prerequisiteEdges.justification: Finding a common multiple to rewrite fractions only makes sense after the learner already treats same-denominator fractions correctly instead of adding both parts.
Percent and decimal forms are equivalent fractions with denominators 100 or powers of ten, so the learner must already generate those equivalents.
Placing a fraction on a marked line requires rewriting it with a denominator that matches the chosen partition.
A ratio becomes a fraction of a whole only after the learner can combine parts into an equivalent whole and simplify.
Sharing requires knowing how many equal parts the whole comprises, which is the part–whole reading of the given ratio.
Practical mix problems often state a concentration as a percent or decimal, so conversion among forms is needed to compute volumes.
Modelling a recipe or mix is the same partition-and-scale procedure applied to authentic quantities and then interpreted.

misconceptions.label: Adds both parts of a fraction
misconceptions.description: When combining or rewriting fractions the learner adds numerators and adds denominators (e.g. 1/2 + 1/3 = 2/5) instead of finding a common denominator or using multiples.

misconceptions.label: Treats percent as a count
misconceptions.description: Reads 16% as the integer 16 or as 16/10 rather than 16/100 when converting among representations.

misconceptions.label: Reads ratio as a subtraction
misconceptions.description: Interprets 2:3 as a difference of 1 rather than as two quantities in a multiplicative relationship.

misconceptions.label: Splits without finding one part
misconceptions.description: When sharing $20 in the ratio 2:3, splits into $2 and $3 (or $10 and $10) instead of finding the value of one of five equal parts.

options.rationale: Multiply numerator and denominator by 2 to get an equivalent fraction.
Adds 2 to both the numerator and the denominator instead of multiplying both by the same number.
Adds 1 to both parts of the fraction rather than using a common multiple.

items.keyRationale: Equivalent fractions are made by multiplying (or dividing) numerator and denominator by the same non-zero whole number.

items.stem: Write 16% as a fraction in simplest form.

options.rationale: 16% means 16/100, which simplifies by dividing by 4 to give 4/25.
Treats the percent as a two-digit whole number over 10 instead of over 100.
Reads 16% as the integer 16 rather than as 16 hundredths.

items.stem: On a number line marked from −2 to 3, which point is halfway between −1 and 2?

options.rationale: The midpoint of −1 and 2 is (−1 + 2)/2 = 1/2.
Chooses the origin instead of averaging the two endpoints.
Averages the absolute values or counts one unit from 0 toward 2.
Takes the negative of the true midpoint.

items.keyRationale: The midpoint of two numbers is their average: (−1 + 2) ÷ 2 = 1/2.

Rejected rather than repaired.

items.stem: In a class the ratio of girls to boys is 2 : 3. What fraction of the class is girls?

options.rationale: There are 2 + 3 = 5 parts in total, so girls are 2 of the 5 parts.
Interprets 2 : 3 as a difference of 1 rather than as parts of a whole.
Uses the part–part ratio as if it were already a part–whole fraction.

items.keyRationale: A part–part ratio 2 : 3 has 5 equal parts in the whole, so the girls are 2/5 of the class.

items.stem: Share $20 in the ratio 2 : 3. How much does the larger share receive?

options.rationale: 2 + 3 = 5 parts; one part is $4; three parts are $12.
Gives the two people $2 and $3 instead of finding the value of one of five equal parts.
Splits the $20 equally rather than in the given ratio.

items.keyRationale: Total parts = 5; $20 ÷ 5 = $4 per part; larger share = 3 × $4 = $12.

items.stem: A cordial mix needs 1 part concentrate to 4 parts water. How many millilitres of concentrate are needed to make 500 mL of drink?

options.rationale: 1 + 4 = 5 parts; 500 ÷ 5 = 100 mL of concentrate.
Divides 500 by 4 and treats water parts only as the whole.
Uses the water share as if it were the concentrate.
Divides 500 by 1 + 4 × 5 or another incorrect grouping of the parts.

items.keyRationale: Five equal parts make 500 mL, so one part of concentrate is 100 mL.
